content:
A problem — the problem? — for first-generation craft breweries is as follows.

1. Everybody knows your iconic beer.
2. Everybody loves your iconic beer.
3. Nobody buys your iconic beer.

We have contemplated this paradox many times here at Hop Take over the years. Recall the disastrous redesign Sapporo USA Sapporo Stone Brewing Sapporo USA put poor Anchor Brewing Company through at the beginning of this decade. Lament the ignominious demise of the original source of Leinenkugel’s beloved shandy. Bear witness to the regrettable unraveling of Rogue Ales & Spirits. And so on and so forth.

Complicating matters, pioneering breweries face a double-bind as they try to breathe new life into old brands. I framed up the problem in January 2023 about New Belgium Brewery’s then-new facelift for Fat Tire:

If Fat Tire were an actual bicycle, most people would put it on Craigslist and call it a day. But New Belgium can’t toss its former glory on the junk heap just yet. Even as younger drinkers gravitate toward the Voodoo Ranger clan’s bolder flavors and packaging, there are plenty of Gen Xers and Millennials with plenty of money for whom Fat Tire represents the golden era of early 21st-century American craft brewing. People still drink it! And despite its diminished stature, Fat Tire is still a top-20 craft brand overall. So New Belgium went for an overhaul instead, reformulating a “crisper, brighter” liquid and giving it a slick new package that calls attention to its eco-friendly credentials and omits its middling 5 percent ABV and outmoded style. “There’s a challenge to recharge heritage brands,” New Belgium vice president of marketing Kyle Bradshaw told Brewbound earlier this month, adding that the move “feels like a big risk” given Fat Tire’s outsized legacy.

That’s the rub. The American drinking public likes the idea of these classic craft beers much more than it actually likes buying them. To tinker with them too much is to invite much nostalgic gnashing of teeth; to leave them entirely untinkered with, to embrace decline.

Next year, Sierra Nevada Brewing Company — purveyor of the eponymous, irreproachable Pale Ale since 1980 — will take its biggest steps yet down the middle path. It’s been a long time coming.

“Five or six years ago when I started with Sierra, you know, one of the things that we were having to overcome was this perception of being ‘grocery store craft,’” says Kyle Ingram, Sierra Nevada’s senior director of innovation, in a phone interview with Hop Take. “Which is not quite an endearing term, not one that we were super proud of.”

The California outfit, which just last year edged out fellow first-waver Boston Beer Company in Brewers Association-defined craft beer barrelage, worked the problem from multiple angles. It recently unveiled its plans to refresh the packaging on a slate of core portfolio brands, including — gasp — Pale Ale itself in fall 2027. “Our portfolio had developed over such a long period of time that it didn’t look coherent on display, and I think some of it had aged and we needed to shake the dust off,” Sierra Nevada chief executive Pryce Greenow explained to Brewbound at a wholesaler conference at its North Carolina plant last month.

It bears mentioning that the company is actually embarking on that tightrope walk from a position of relative strength. According to multi-outlet grocery, mass retail, and convenience stores tracked by the market-research firm Circana, Sierra Nevada’s portfolio grew 1.9 percent in dollars and 0.2 percent in case volume year-to-date through September 6, outpacing the declining category and the even-more-rapidly declining craft segment within it.

Perhaps emboldened by that trend-bucking performance, the invigoration effort won’t stop with refreshes, though. “When you have a healthy core, it allows you to innovate in a way where we’re not dependent on that [new] thing being big and successful right out of the gate,” says Ingram.

To that end, Sierra Nevada has cued up two of its boldest portfolio expansions in recent memory. Crafted By Sierra Nevada, a line featuring “spiked agave seltzer” (read: hard seltzer) Agua Azul and “beer soda” (read: radler) Shred, marks the firm’s first major foray into the “beyond beer” space since it spun up and wound down also-ran entrants Tea West and Strainge Beast earlier this decade. The new fermentables are already on (or soon to hit) shelves in test markets bearing subordinated branding from the mothership.

“The question has always been can we win in those spaces without leveraging the awareness and the credibility of the Sierra Nevada brand, but also to do so without disparaging or diluting the equity of the Sierra Nevada brand for a loyal beer drinker?” says Ingram, to whom fell the unenviable responsibility of pitching founder Ken Grossman on a beer soda called Shred. “I remember thinking distinctly, this might be my last pitch,” he tells Hop Take, laughing.

Whether Craft By Sierra Nevada’s offerings can thrive — or even survive — in a lucrative-but-tricky flavored malt beverage pseudosegment dominated by scaled flavor-chasers like Mark Anthony Group, Anheuser-Busch InBev, and BBC remains to be seen. But to your humble Hop Take columnist’s eye, the thesis on those products is sound.

This brings us to the Hidden Scroll series. Unlike Crafted By, this new “brand family” is composed of honest-to-goodness beers, but it is tasked with a more ambitious goal. Namely: to score big, consistent Sierra Nevada some of the lucre and latter-day cachet of small, dynamic “hype breweries.”

“That guy who is paying 25 bucks for a four-pack, he’s looking for some of the more local, the more ‘hype’ kind of breweries in that space,” says Ingram. “We’re certainly capable and credible from a brewing standpoint, but maybe that’s not the area of the shelf or the cooler where people are looking for Sierra Nevada.” Building on the promise of West Ghost India Pale Ale — a semi-branded offering that made the transition from taproom-only bestseller to national packaged distribution in early 2026 — the company has formalized its higher-pricepoint ambitions under Hidden Scroll, so named because beers under this aegis will not feature the venerable gold sheafing that adorns labels in the core portfolio.

“That’s the first thing we want people to see, it’s the thing that brings that credibility, but we weren’t sure that it was working to our advantage in this space,” says Ingram of the scroll design. Instead: “Let’s grab shoppers’ attention with really cool modern artwork, because that’s a lot of how these guys shop.” He should know — by his own admission, he’s one of them.

For 2027, Sierra Nevada has retooled West Ghost’s packaging, and is deliberating over which of the other Hidden Scrolls beers it’s been testing in its taprooms it will put into 4-packs and push into distribution. Potential options include Boat Plane, a West Coast Pilsner, and Lava Lamp, a double IPA. The cans feature art-forward designs printed on the white matte labeling that’s become a visual lingua franca among more specialty craft offerings. There’s very little obvious connection to the brewery from whence they came but for a “Sierra Nevada Brewing Co., Chico, CA & Mills River, NC” demarcation along the bottom in small letters, and a faint scroll that’s been blended — hidden — into the illustration.

“People aren’t grabbing it because it’s from Sierra Nevada, they’re finding out that it’s from Sierra Nevada after they’ve already thrown a couple back,” says Ingram. “It’s been wildly successful for us, relative to the size of the category. We had a hard time keeping up with the volume in the first few months.”

Here, another rub. A core appeal of “hype” beers — to the extent that such appeal still exists at scale as we enter the back half of the ‘20s — is their scarcity, esotericism, and rapid-fire release cadence. Would, say, Other Half Brewing Company’s offerings have captivated finance bros late last decade if they were available in a dozen states, rather than only via a hole-in-the-wall across the street from a McDonald’s in central Brooklyn? Or, asked another way, is that sort of “hype” compatible with a Sierra Nevada sort of craft brewery?

I ask Ingram to square this circle.

For all Sierra Nevada’s logistical and technical advantages, “we have some disadvantages too. We’re not built to do small things really, really fast,” he concedes. “We’re not really designed to. That’s not the game that we’re playing, but we still feel like we can have a meaningful place in this category.”

Can Hidden Scroll find a place among the hype beer pantheon? Can Crafted By Sierra Nevada succeed where previous beyond-beer bids have failed? Can this four-decade firm bust the double-bind that has hemmed in so many craft beer brands of a certain age? Sierra Nevada has put together a compelling case. But only John Q. Guzzler can make the call.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

It’s no secret that Boston Beer Company has struggled mightily marketing-wise over the past few years. So the fact that it has a new chief marketing officer lined up isn’t surprising. But Allison Stransky, who starts October 12, has a resume that ought to raise some eyebrows: she’s taking this job after serving as the marketing lead for Samsung Electronics America. Can you pitch Samuel Adams the same way you pitch smartphones? Trade wisdom holds that you cannot. But we’ll see!

BBC taproom workers in Boston voted “overwhelmingly” to join the Teamsters… The THC drinks industry scored a brief stay of execution earlier this month when President Trump signed a bill kicking the can(nabis) to mid-December… New Belgium Brewery announced plans to open a “Liquid Center” (i.e., taproom) at Voodoo Ranger’s plant in Virginia…

📉 …and downs

Farewell to Mary Guiver, the longtime beer lead at Whole Foods Market, who’s moving to another role within the Amazon-owned grocer… Tilray Brands partnered with Spirit Halloween for a Shock Top promotion nobody asked for… More tough news from the Twin Cities, where top-50 firm Summit Brewing faces foreclosure… Rest in peace to Triple Rock, the country’s longest continuously operating brewpub, which is slated to shut its doors in Berkeley…

content:
The Espresso Martini is one of the most popular cocktails of today. The modern classic — featuring vodka, coffee liqueur, espresso, and simple syrup — has solidified itself as a go-to for partygoers and casual sippers alike. And with the high demand for Espresso Martinis at every bar and brunch destination comes the question of how prices for the cocktail compare across the U.S.

To track the current state of Espresso Martini prices across the country, VinePair tapped insights company Ground Signal to find the coffee cocktail’s average cost in each state. Ground Signal — which provides artificial intelligence-powered data to help beverage-alcohol brands to boost their on-premise sales — surveyed menus across the country to compare how the on-premise price for the drink varies state-by-state.

Hawaii leads the U.S. with the most expensive Espresso Martini on average at $16.92. Though it’s the only state to commercially produce coffee, goods in Hawaii are generally more expensive as shipping commodities to the island racks up costs. Just behind it is New York at $16.03. The two are the only states with average Espresso Martini prices above $16. Rounding out the top five are Nevada ($15.94), California ($15.57), and Washington, D.C. ($15.38).

The average cost for the classic cocktail across the entire U.S. is $14.38, and only 15 states post a mean price above the national average.

So, which states shake up the most affordable Espresso Martini? Oklahoma takes home the title, with an average cost of just $12.06, with South Dakota ($12.40) and Iowa ($12.43) claiming the second and third spots. Rounding out the five least-expensive states for the coffee cocktail are Nebraska and Mississipppi, where it costs $12.50 on average.

Ground Signal also found the brands for vodka — which is the spirit of choice in 90 percent of the country’s Espresso Martinis — most common in each state. Tito’s was the top vodka brand in 29 states, with Ketel One representing the top pick in 17 states. Stoli was the go-to in five states, and Absolut in one.

title: A Restaurant’s Off-Menu Wine List Should Feel Special, Not Exclusive
summary:
When I travel, I tend to go a bit extreme in my research of where I should eat and drink. Years ago, before taking a trip to Amsterdam, it was no different. During my weeks of research, I stumbled upon a new spot whose Instagram feed was chock full of wine nerd clickbait, but one post in particular caught my eye: “These Gems are Hiding in Our Wine Room: Kenjiro Kagami’s Domaine des Miroirs.” Naturally, I wanted to raid that wine room.

content:
When I travel, I tend to go a bit extreme in my research of where I should eat and drink. Years ago, before taking a trip to Amsterdam, it was no different. During my weeks of research, I stumbled upon a new spot whose Instagram feed was chock full of wine nerd clickbait, but one post in particular caught my eye: “These Gems are Hiding in Our Wine Room: Kenjiro Kagami’s Domaine des Miroirs.” Naturally, I wanted to raid that wine room.

We arrived at the restaurant and cafe, and I dug through the list only to find it was not there. I assumed someone had the same idea I had, came in, and bought it. I could find another wine, but I had to ask. What followed was my first true experience with the “off list” wine. It was an interrogation, albeit a very kind and hospitable one.

“How do you know this wine?”

“What do you know about this wine and its winemaker?”

“Have you ever had this wine before?”

“Are there other producers from this region that you really love?”

“What other wines are you really into right now?”

“Are there other wines that you see on the list that interest you?”

Some of these questions were things a somm may ask a guest when trying to figure out what wines to suggest, but this was different. It was a test, a very polite test, but a test all the same. Ultimately, I passed, after which it was explained, apologetically, that the restaurant only received a few bottles a year and they wanted to make sure each went to someone who would appreciate it.

The wine was great, the meal was great, and the service was solid. Overall, it was a great meal, though, to be honest, it did strike me as a bit odd and a little off-putting in the beginning. While this wine was definitely culty and nerdy at that time, it had yet to reach the unicorn status it has now. They did post the wine publicly, and that alone would attract people who appreciate it. It was most likely meant to bring in wine lovers like myself to the space, so why gatekeep it?

I’d mostly forgotten about this experience until a friend told me about something similar that had recently happened to him in Manhattan.

He went to a well known restaurant, and one of the servers recognized him immediately as a wine professional and let him know they had some amazing “off list” wines. He ordered one of the wines and loved it. He went back a few weeks later and inquired about the wine, but this time he had a different server.

“That wine isn’t on the list. Where did you have it?”

“Here.”

“Who served it to you?”

“Another server, I don’t remember his name.”

“Here?”

“Yes, here.”

After a pause, there was a, “Yeah, we have it.”

Mind you, this was not a unicorn $500 bottle with only two cases imported to the United States. It was a sub $100 wine from an unsung appellation. Needless to say, it left a bit of a bad taste in my friend’s mouth.

I was amazed by the absurdity and frustration of it, but the story brought me back to Amsterdam. What would my experience have been if I hadn’t answered the questions correctly? Would they have denied me? How would I have felt? Would I have been embarrassed? One thing is certain: I would not have felt better about myself or my experience at the restaurant, and I’m guessing others would not feel great about it either.

I want to lay this out from a hospitality perspective. I’m of the school that everyone should get a wonderful and equitable experience at a restaurant or bar, and that everyone should feel like they are getting something special. Having a separate list just for regulars and wine nerds goes against that.

Daniel Eddy of Brooklyn’s celebrated Winner and Runner Up has long talked about having a separate list, though he doesn’t view the potential list as a secret. He looks at it in a similar way to a rewards program punch card. If a guest dines with them five or 10 times, they would “unlock” a special list with rare, allocated bottles at a fair, nongouged price. He sees the possibility as more of a known reward for consistent patronage.

His reasoning is that he has a pretty deep list of special, hard to get wines at below market prices. Some are his personal consignments. When he first opened, there were several guests who would come in, cherry pick all the special wines, and never come back again. “I’d rather reward those who become regulars than let the cherry-pickers clean out the list and never return,” he says. As of today, he has not implemented this strategy but hopes to someday soon.

I get it. Wine directors don’t get many bottles of certain wines, and they want them to go to people who will both enjoy and appreciate them. You also want your regulars to feel special, but I don’t love the practice. How do you handle the guest who asks for the “secret list,” but isn’t a regular or someone you know? They clearly know about the list. They’re asking. How can you be hospitable in that situation?

I know of a restaurant where somms are instructed to tell guests a listed bottle is 86’d if the wine director doesn’t know the guest or thinks they don’t “deserve” the wine. It’s crazy to me that this happens, but sadly it does, and this type of gatekeeping is exactly why wine is struggling these days.

If you list a wine, everyone should be able to buy it, regardless of their knowledge of wine. Most guests who come in aren’t going to know as much as the somm, and yes, the somm can and should try to steer people toward wines they think the guest will love and away from wines they may not enjoy as much. But if the guest sees something on the list and wants to pay for it, it should not be withheld. It’s bad business among other things.

None of this is without caveats. I would be lying if I said I never sold off-list wines. I have. At my restaurant LaLou, we had plenty of wines that were not listed for a variety of reasons.

Some wines needed time and were purposely held in the cellar until we thought they were ready to go. Occasionally, someone would come in and want that particular style of wine. We might sell them a bottle with the understanding that “it might be a bit tight” or “it’s a bit young, but let’s see where it’s at.”

Some wine lists only have a limited amount of space, and some places will keep wines off because they simply don’t have room and are waiting for another wine to run out before they can print it. I would 100 percent sell that wine off-list to a guest who was looking for something similar. Sometimes I would sell wines that had just arrived and we had not had time to list them, but I would sell the wine based on the guest’s preferences, not on who the guest was or what they did or didn’t know about the wine.

It’s important to note that these wines were not on a separate “cool kids,” industry or regulars list. They were offered to any guests who were not finding what they wanted on our list, and we were attempting to give them a special experience. It wasn’t a strategic “special list” for certain guests. It was happenstance that allowed us to do this, and I think that is the main point.

Here, it’s the intent that counts. Hospitality is giving people something they didn’t know they wanted. A special list for the worthy or those in the know is antithetical to that. It doesn’t create new regulars, it rewards the current ones while running the risk of alienating potential ones.

At a moment when we are barraged with stories that hospitality is at a breaking point and wine consumption is at a breaking point, that restaurants are going out of business, and grape growers are ripping out vines, we should be thinking of ways to get more people in the doors and drinking more wine, not excluding guests and potential wine drinkers.

News to know:

  • California’s longest family-run winery files for bankruptcy: Gundlach Bundschu Winery, the oldest continuously family-run producer in the state, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. After 168 years in business, the winery, known among devotees as GunBun, is now seeking an investor to reorganize its finances and remain afloat.
  • Stateside, AB InBev dismiss suit over packaging dupe: Stateside Brands and Anheuser-Busch InBev agreed to dismiss lawsuit over lookalike spiked tea brands on Monday. In a filing last October, Stateside accused AB InBev of mimicking “the overall look and feel” of Surfside’s vodka tea cans with its similar ready-to-drink (RTD) brand Skimmers. The judge also waived all rights to appeal, as first reported by BrewBound.
  • White Claw maker pivots to Reyes in Denver: Mark Anthony Brands, which owns popular RTDs like White Claw and The Finnish Long Drink, exited Coors Distributing Company and pivoted to a Reyes subsidiary as its distributor in Denver. The producer will now distribute via Reyes Beverage Group (RBG) Spirits and Wine of Colorado. The switchover is the latest win for RBG, which picked up the majority of RNDC’s former accounts this year.

Product releases to watch:

  • Compass Box’s latest U.S. release blends three 10-year-old whiskies: The popular blended Scotch brand introduced “This is a 10-Year-Old Whisky” — a combination of three, decade-old single malts — to U.S. markets. The limited-edition blend is now available for purchase online for $84.99.
  • Laphroaig cements 15-year-old single malt in U.S. portfolio: The Islay Scotch brand is bringing back Laphroaig 15-Year-Old Single Malt Scotch Whisky to U.S. markets as a permanent addition to its lineup after over a decade away. Laphroaig aged the expression in ex-bourbon casks for 15 years before bottling at 92 proof. Laphroaig 15-Year-Old Single Malt Scotch Whisky is now available nationwide for a suggested retail price of $89.

content:
From the boozy and caffeinated Espresso Martini to the provocative, passion fruit-spiked Pornstar Martini, many of the bar world’s most beloved modern classics were invented in London. But beyond these household names there’s another London-born cocktail that’s been largely flying under the radar — though it might be ready for its main character moment.

The East 8 Hold-Up, a humble combination of vodka, Aperol, lime juice, pineapple juice, simple syrup, and passion fruit syrup, recently ranked No. 45 on Drinks International’s annual list of the most popular cocktails in the world. Sandwiched between beloved, well-known concoctions like the Piña Colada and the Vieux Carré, its inclusion on the list might seem to have come out of left-field. But the cocktail is far from new. Created in 2010, the East 8 Hold-Up has been quietly gaining steam over the years, likely winning over fans with its approachable flavor profile, recognizable ingredients, and bright color.

Bartender Kevin Armstrong first mixed up the drink at Milk & Honey’s London location. Londoners and others familiar with the city probably understand the connotations that the “East 8,” colloquially known as E8, neighborhood holds: At the time, it was a rough-around-the-edges area of the city, riddled with robberies and other crime.

In 2010, Armstrong was brainstorming ways to create new and exciting spins on cocktails served in a traditional format. During the first eight years of the bar’s run, most of its menus featured classic cocktails without much innovation, Armstrong told the magazine “Australian Bartender” in a 2010 interview. When it was his turn to write the menu, he wanted to add a new, modern vodka cocktail that followed a similar format to old-school drinks.

During that time, Armstrong and fellow bartender Sam Jeveons were venturing home after a night out together. Armstrong, who’d lived in East 8 at the time, had just parted ways with Jeveons when the latter stopped to, well, “take a leak.” While relieving himself with his pants around his ankles, a man approached him from behind, stepped on his pants, and demanded his wallet.

As Armstrong tells it: Rather than letting the robber get away with his wallet, Jeveons chased the thief around East 8 with his pants down to his ankles. The bit became known as the East 8 Hold-Up between the two of them.

Though the event itself has little to do with the build of the cocktail, the incident provided a catchy name for Armstrong’s vodka-based creation. The drink combines vodka, Aperol, pineapple and lime juices, and simple and passion fruit syrups, shaken until it develops a frothy texture. The bright orange concoction — which gets its color from the combination of Aperol and passion fruit — is poured over ice in a rocks glass, garnished with a duo of pineapple and lime wedges. The cocktail is tangy and fruity — but not overwhelmingly so, as the heft of the vodka and bitterness of Aperol balance out the syrups and juices.

According to Drinks International, the East 8 Hold-Up has gained traction among contemporary drinks savants worldwide. While not quite a household name yet, the drink can be found on an increasing number of craft cocktail menus. Bars like Satan’s Whiskers and Café Clement in London offer the drink, but the East 8 Hold-Up also crossed the pond and landed on the menu at Beef & Liberty Bar, the cocktail haunt above Hawksmoor’s Chicago location.

The East 8 Hold-Up isn’t the only British beverage that’s recently gained traction in international markets, especially in the U.S. The Gimlet, which was famously invented for the British Royal Navy, is enjoying a heyday among a certain set of drinkers. And one of New York City’s hottest newcomers, Dean’s, serves oysters over a shot of Guinness, a time-tested pub classic. What’s next for the “British Invasion” in stateside bars and restaurants? Expect the East 8 Hold-Up to round the corner.

title: The VinePair Podcast: Has Collecting Gone From Cool to Cringe?
summary:

Glenmorangie 50 Years Old was non-chill filtered and bottled at 45.7 percent ABV (91.4 proof). Brand tasting notes highlight baking spices, toffee, and leather on the nose. The palate brings pepper, tea leaves, grape must, and oak tannin, leading into a long, spice-forward finish.

The distillery commissioned renowned ceramicists Peter and Laurie Pincus to create the sleek porcelain package design. The pair developed an elegant, oval-shaped vessel that features 50 different colors as a nod to the whisky’s age.

The exceedingly exclusive bottling — only 149 numbered bottles of Glenmorangie 50 Years Old exist — hit the market for a suggested retail price of £25,800 ($36,000). It is available to select retailers, through Moët Hennessy Private Client Team network, and at the distillery’s visitor center in Tain, Scotland.

content:
Chardonnay is one of the world’s most popular grape varieties, but not every bottle is created equally. With the grape’s wide range of expressions and price points, it can sometimes seem difficult to find the middle ground between the ultra-rich, overly oaky budget bottles and the more nuanced, terroir-driven wines with daunting price tags.

But you don’t have to spend a fortune to explore all that Chardonnay has to offer beyond the notorious butter bombs that once gave the grape a bad name. To help pinpoint which bottles deliver the ample quality without the sticker shock that can come with high-end Chardonnay, we asked nine sommeliers from across the country which bottles they think offer the most bang for your buck. From surprisingly affordable White Burgundy to complex Chardonnays from buzzy Oregon producers, here are their picks for the best value Chardonnays.

The best bang-for-your-buck Chardonnays, according to sommeliers:

  • Lioco Sonoma Coast Chardonnay
  • On Wine Hill “Millerandage” Chardonnay 2024
  • Brij Wines Chardonnay
  • Enfield Wine Co. Citrine Chardonnay
  • Enfield Wine Co. Brosseau Chardonnay
  • Evening Land Vineyards Seven Springs Chardonnay
  • Lingua Franca Avni Chardonnay 2024
  • Scar of the Sea SLO Coast Chardonnay 2024
  • Domaine des Terres de Chatenay Mâcon-Villages “La Cuvée de Béracius” 2025

“I’m quite fond of the Lioco Sonoma Coast Chardonnay. It’s an unoaked style that tends to show bright acidity and some Chablis-like qualities. Generally, you can get it for around $25 retail, and it’s from a small, family-run winery.” —Gregory Wilson, sommelier, Beckon, Denver

“When it comes to delicious and affordable Chardonnay, so much great wine is being made on the West Coast right now. One of my favorites that has caught my attention lately is the On Wine Hill “Millerandage” Chardonnay 2024 from the Willamette Valley, Ore. Jeff Vejr is doing some really cool things in Oregon, and for this particular wine, he is using a specific clone (548) of Chardonnay that is predisposed to what is known as ‘millerandage’ or ‘hens and chicks.’ This causes uneven ripening of the grape clusters so some berries will be larger while others remain small. This increases the skin-to-juice ratio, giving the wine a beautiful, finely grained texture, as well as a natural kick of acidity from the tart, smaller berries in the bunch. This wine has the textural richness to hold up to a variety of foods, but it’s also fresh and fun enough to be enjoyed on its own!” —Cameron Dellinger, wine director, Jungsik, New York City

“I would love to shout out the Chardonnay from Brij Wines from the San Luis Obispo Coast. This project, from renowned California winemaker and master sommelier Raj Parr, uses fruit purchased from local growers who share his passion for sustainable farming. The winemaking is as thoughtful and non-interventionist as you find in any of the bottlings at Parr Wines but at a fraction of the price, typically retailing around $35. The wine itself has the rich texture and subtle oak aromas that I’m looking for in a California Chardonnay, but with salinity and freshness that speak to the wine’s coastal origins.” —Audrey Dowling, beverage director, Rye Bunny, Washington, D.C.

“I’ve always had a soft spot in my heart for the wines of Enfield Wine Company and found they’ve always delivered far beyond its price point. Winemaker John Lockwood comes from the pedigree of Littorai and Failla, two wineries that I would define as American winemaking excellence, as well as a commitment to working with small farmers in select California heritage sites that stand out to him. At $30 retail, the Citrine is far from the traditional California Chardonnay that has left a bad taste in the mouth of many wine drinkers, but offers a soft touch of yellow apple and citrus with a round tropical finish bursting with a kiss of saline minerality. Just writing about the wine makes me want to open another bottle from Enfield sooner than later.” —Angel Prado, lead sommelier, Sorelle, Charleston

“I love the Enfield Wine Co. Brosseau Chardonnay. It’s planted on super high elevation, limestone soils in Chalone, giving it this really distinct California terroir. There’s lean, mineral, acidity but it finishes lush, savory, round, and complex. It’s a great wine to get you from start to finish in the meal. The winemakers are really excited to be sharing the unique terroirs of California while celebrating dedicated farmers and growers in the region.” —Charlotte Mirzoeff, general manager and beverage director, Arthur, Brooklyn

“I think Evening Land Vineyards Chardonnay ‘Seven Springs’ from Eola Amity Hills, Ore. is the best affordable Chardonnay. At around $29 retail, this wine is as close to Meursault as you can find in the U.S. and at a fraction of the cost. It’s slightly reductive, just ripe enough and loaded with the savory mineral notes that are the backbone of all great Chardonnays.” —Francesco Grosso, wine director, Ai Fiori, NYC

“The current belief that the best place outside Burgundy to grow Chardonnay is the Willamette Valley, Ore. I have consistently been pleased with the Burgundian character of Chardonnays from Willamette Valley. My favorite is Lingua Franca Avni Chardonnay 2024, made by cherished Burgundy winemaker Dominique Lafon and Master Sommelier Larry Stone, with protégé Thomas Savre. It tastes like dipping your toe in a Meursault.” —Lindsey Geddes, wine director, Carversteak, Las Vegas

“With Scar of the Sea SLO Coast Chardonnay, you’re getting a bright and fresh expression of coastal California Chardonnay, with a long élevage and incredible farming practices. It has energy and depth, and punches way above its price point!” —Shanna Nasiri, owner, With Others, Brooklyn

“Domaine des Terres de Chatenay Mâcon-Villages ‘La Cuvée de Béracius’ 2025. I’m always excited to find a White Burgundy that overdelivers, and this old-vine Mâcon-Villages from Jean-Claude and Marie-Odile Janin is one I keep coming back to. Made from 70-year-old Chardonnay vines planted in the clay-limestone soils of Péronne, it has vibrant fruit, chalky minerality, and incredible tension. It has the focus and depth I love in great Burgundy while still feeling fresh and distinctive, so much so that we carry it at Le Pavillon. This limited-production cuvée is that rarest of finds: a true ‘unicorn’ wine from the Mâconnais.” —John Osborne, head sommelier, Le Pavillon, NYC

content:
This article is part of our Cocktail Chatter series, where we dive into the wild, weird, and wondrous corners of history to share over a cocktail and impress your friends.

The French baguette is losing steam: From 1970 to 2022, the number of traditional boulangeries in France dropped by roughly 400 a year from about 55,000 to 35,000. In response, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) granted the French baguette its Intangible Cultural Heritage designation to preserve the tradition of breadmaking.

Though the numbers might suggest this culinary staple is waning, there still appears to be no shortage of baguettes in the country. In Paris, pedestrians will see locals and tourists alike walking the streets with the loaf of bread in tow, either clutched under the arm or poking out of a bag. The city also hosts a prestigious annual competition to find the best baguette in Paris, in which over 100 bakers submit their best loaves to be measured, weighed, and tasted for a chance to win a cash prize and a one-year contract to be the exclusive baguette supplier to the French president’s residence. But for those looking to experience the country’s carb culture in the most authentic way, there’s only one type of baguette to order.

The best baguettes slung around Paris are of a certain, government-controlled variety, thanks to a French law passed in 1993. The 1993 décret du pain (the bread decree), which sought to protect the sacred practice of breadmaking, legislated that baguettes labeled “tradition” must be made with just wheat flour, water, salt, and yeast or sourdough starter — no preservatives or other additives. The dough can also never be frozen, and the baguettes must be baked on the site where they are sold. “Baguettes de tradition” is the only government-controlled bread category.

The designation works much like the Appellation d’Origine Contrôlée (AOC) system, which mandates that wines labeled under a given region must follow specific quality and production standards, such as permitting certain grapes, aging methods, and additives. Similarly, at boulangeries around the country, loaves of bread are often placed into different baskets, with each label corresponding to the respective variety.

Ordering a stick from the tradition — aptly named and easy to remember, as it is the most traditional variety — basket ensures you’ll be eating the highest-quality bread, one with a craggly and sturdy exterior that opens to a bouncy, stretchy interior. Flavors of toasted and fresh yeast will be strong throughout.

Other baguette varieties include the “baguette classique” (also labeled as “ordinaire”) and the “baguette aux céréales” (also labeled as “aux graines”). A classique is a run-of-the-mill baguette, not protected under any government regulations, meaning the dough could have been frozen or it could contain preservatives to elongate its shelf life. A baguette aux céréales is the multigrain version of a baguette, with seeds and grains studding the loaf.

When ordering a baguette — whether de tradition or not — there are some other ways to communicate with the boulanger to ensure the bread will suit your specifications. Those who like sturdy, crunchy bread can ask for one bien cuite, or well cooked. Those who like a softer and more chewy loaf can ask for one pas trop cuite, or not too cooked. In either case, the baker will inspect their loaves and hand you the one that best suits your needs.

Whether mass-produced or not, any baguette in France is likely to be tasty and to evoke warm, happy feelings of European life. But when traveling the country, ordering your bread à la française can elevate that feeling, one yeasty crunch at a time.

content:
Dating back to the late-1800s, the Manhattan is widely considered the first “modern” cocktail. It’s an incredibly simple formula of whiskey, sweet vermouth, and a couple dashes of bitters, and if you stick to the script, the only room for customization comes from choosing between spicy rye and rich bourbon.

While the cocktail is relatively straightforward, its effortless balance gave way to numerous variations. It also inspired a new category of cocktails made by mixing spirits with fortified wine that have become classics in their own right like the Rob Roy or Vieux Carré.

Since bartenders have been riffing on this cocktail for over a century, we tapped a few to see how they put their own twist on the Manhattan when making the drink at home. From swapping vermouth for a rich amaro to sneaking in other spirits like mezcal, here’s how nine top bartenders make Manhattans at home.

Kyle Jackson

Bar director, Markette and The Argyle, New York City

For a Manhattan at home, I don’t think there’s much reason to reinvent it. The drink is iconic because of its simplicity, so for me, it comes down to choosing ingredients that each bring something specific. I use Michter’s rye because it has the spice and complexity I want from a rye, but also a lingering finish that carries through the vermouth instead of disappearing underneath it. For the sweet vermouth, I go with Noilly Prat Rouge. French sweet vermouth might be a slightly controversial choice for a Manhattan, but I prefer the finesse of Noilly Prat here. It gives the drink enough richness and herbal character without becoming too assertive. My spec is also very easy to remember: 2:1:2, which conveniently happens to be Manhattan’s original area code.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces Michter’s Rye Whiskey
  • 1 ounce Noilly Prat Rouge sweet vermouth
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • Garnish: cherry and orange oil

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled Martini glass. Garnish with a cherry, then express an orange peel over the surface of the drink and discard the peel.

Owen Gibler

Partner and beverage director, Bar Roza, Nashville

When making drinks at home, avoiding pitfalls creates a more measurable change than aiming for exotic tweaks. Pitfall one: vermouth. Every article mentioning a vermouth cocktail should include a disclaimer noting that it is a fortified wine and oxidizes quickly. The trick is to make lots of Manhattans and never have a bottle open for more than a week. Pitfall two: ice. Home ice is generally smaller and melts faster than a cocktail bar’s ice, so use less ice and a shorter stir. And pitfall three: warm glassware. Stick your coupe into the freezer for a few minutes before using it. It’s such an easy move that creates a dramatic improvement.

Ingredients

  • 2 ¼ ounces Woody Creek Rye
  • ¾ ounce Cocchi Vermouth di Torino
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • Garnish: cherry

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients into a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled coupe and garnish with a cherry.

James Grant

Beverage director, Fairmont Royal York, Toronto, Canada

I love a Manhattan. More specifically, I love experimenting with a Manhattan. The classic specification of two parts whiskey to one part sweet vermouth finished with a couple of dashes of bitters is certainly serviceable, but the simple formula can sometimes feel a little bare-bones or thin. I typically gravitate toward cocktails such as a Black Manhattan, À La Louisiane, Bobby Burns, or Tipperary, which introduce an added layer of complexity through the inclusion of a liqueur. With that in mind, when I make a Manhattan at home, I tend to dress it up slightly with the addition of an amaro. I choose one that complements both the herbal profile of the vermouth and the character of the whiskey. That touch of sweetness also provides a little extra body, helping to keep the cocktail from feeling too lean.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces Lot No. 40 Rye Whisky
  • 1 ounce Cocchi Storico Vermouth di Torino
  • ¼ ounce Amaro Meletti
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • 2 dashes orange bitters
  • Garnish: brandied cherry and orange oil

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled Nick & Nora glass. Garnish with a brandied cherry, then express an orange peel over the surface of the drink and discard the peel.

Johnisha Williams

Bar manager, Commander’s Palace, New Orleans

I like a perfect Manhattan because using both sweet and dry vermouth gives the drink a nice balance while still letting the rye shine. I also like using both Angostura and Peychaud’s as a little nod to New Orleans and how we make our Sazerac here at Commander’s. The Angostura gives it that familiar spice, while the Peychaud’s adds a lighter, floral note. I also really enjoy rye as an introduction to the whiskey world. I personally don’t typically reach for bourbon, and I find rye to be a little easier and more approachable for someone who doesn’t normally drink whiskey. It still has that depth and character you expect from whiskey, but I find the spice and overall profile makes it an enjoyable starting point. For me, a Manhattan is a great way to introduce someone to rye without asking them to drink it neat or on the rocks.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces rye whiskey
  • ½ ounce sweet vermouth
  • ½ ounce dry vermouth
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • 1 dash Peychaud’s bitters
  • Garnish: lemon twist

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients into a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a child coupe or Nick and Nora glass. Garnish with a lemon twist.

Chuck Worley

Bar manager, Lowland, Charleston

This vision was born out of my love for mezcal. I love a split base, booze-forward cocktail, so I’m using equal parts mezcal and a sweeter rye, pulling back the sweet vermouth just a touch, throwing in a couple dashes of classic bitters and a small bar spoon of Luxardo cherry juice.

Ingredients

  • 1 ¼ ounces Banhez mezcal
  • 1 ¼ ounces Angel’s Envy Rye
  • ½ ounce Carpano Antica Formula
  • 4 dashes Angostura bitters
  • 1 bar spoon of Luxardo cherry syrup
  • Ganish: Luxardo cherry and orange oil

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled coupe glass. Garnish with a Luxardo cherry, then express an orange peel over the surface of the drink and discard the peel.

Kristine Nguyen

Head bartender, Bludorn, Houston

This is a riff on a Black Manhattan with pandan adding a subtle tropical note and amaro bringing enough bitterness to keep the drink grounded. I’ve always enjoyed Black Manhattans because they give you so much room to play with the level and style of bitterness. This recipe is meant to do the same.

Ingredients

  • 1 ½ ounces Tres Tribus Mezcal
  • ¾ ounce Foro Amaro
  • ½ ounce sweet vermouth
  • 1 bar spoon Kota pandan liqueur
  • Garnish: lemon twist

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a coupe or your preferred glass. Garnish with lemon twist.

Austin Krudys

Beverage manager, The Chloe, Nashville

My go-to Manhattan is a Black Manhattan, a simple twist on the classic recipe that swaps out sweet vermouth for Averna amaro. The Averna introduces a unique layer of complexity, leaning a bit more bitter and herbaceous. As a bonus for home bartenders, Averna doesn’t require refrigeration like sweet vermouth does, giving it a much longer shelf life.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces high-proof rye like Rittenhouse Rye
  • 1 ounce Averna amaro
  • 2 dashes Regan’s orange bitters
  • Garnish: Luxardo cherry

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled Nick & Nora glass. Garnish with a Luxardo cherry.

Oscar Valle

Co-founder, TONANA, San Miguel de Allende, Mexico

My go-to at home is a 50/50 Manhattan with Angostura bitters. I love that ratio because it gives the vermouth as much room to shine as the whiskey. Its herbal notes and sweetness balance the spice of the rye, while the Angostura brings everything together. The orange twist adds a bright aroma that lifts the drink. It’s simple to make at home with no special prep. Just remember to keep your vermouth refrigerated after opening so it stays fresh.

Ingredients

  • 1½ ounces rye whiskey
  • 1½ ounces sweet vermouth
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • Garnish: orange twist

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled coupe or Nick & Nora glass. Express the oils from an orange twist over the drink and use it as the garnish.

Carlo Olcese

Co-owner and director of operations, Bateman’s, NYC

Whenever I make a Manhattan at home, I lean toward the bittersweet twist of a Black Manhattan, replacing sweet vermouth with Averna amaro. The benefit is that I don’t have to worry about stocking fresh vermouth in my fridge every month. I use Angel’s Envy Kentucky Straight Bourbon since its vanilla notes pair incredibly well with the anise flavor of Averna. To finish, I add one dash of Angostura bitters for some baking spice, and about a half spoon of Luxardo cherry syrup to add a touch of sweetness. Once the drink has been poured, I drop a Luxardo cherry at the bottom for a sweet treat at the end of my drink.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces Angel’s Envy Kentucky Straight Bourbon
  • 1 ounce Averna Amaro
  • 1 dash Angostura bitters
  • ½ bar spoon Luxardo maraschino cherry syrup
  • Garnish: Luxardo cherry

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled, stemmed glass. Garnish with a Luxardo cherry.

content:
Though many consumers might recognize tequila as what they encountered in a shot in college or as the ingredient in their favorite cocktail, there’s also a market for extremely high-end tequila.

These luxury bottles, often from prestigious brands like Clase Azul and Patrón, are revered for both their flavor profiles and elaborate presentations — many are sold in artisanal decanters made in collaboration with esteemed artists. But beyond the substance of what’s in the bottle and style of the packaging, exclusivity is also a factor in the premium tequila market: The most coveted bottlings often come from limited-production runs of under 500 bottles in total.

From anniversary releases to extra añejos, here are the most expensive tequilas in the world, according to Wine Searcher.

10. Clase Azul Eduardo Sarabia Limited Edition Tequila Joven, Jalisco, Mexico

Clase Azul collaborated with Mexican-American contemporary artist Eduard Sarabia for this limited-edition release. This Joven blend — of which only 450 exist — combines Clase Azul blanco, Russian oak-aged añejo, and sherry cask-aged añejo.

  • Average price: $8,691
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Citrus, vanilla, caramel

9. Patrón Limited Edition En Lalique Serie 2 Tequila Extra Añejo, Jalisco, Mexico

The second edition of Patrón’s En Lalique series — released in 2017 — was aged for eight years in American oak, French oak, and ex-sherry barrels with just 299 bottles hitting markets.

  • Average price: $8,839
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Honey, citrus fruit, oak

8. Clase Azul Puebla Limited Edition Tequila, Jalisco, Mexico

This extra-aged tequila from Clase Azul, which matures in antique French barrels, is produced as an homage to the Battle of Puebla. There are only 300 hand-numbered bottles in existence.

  • Average price: $9,358
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Baking spice, dried fruit, toasted oak

7. Dos Armadillos ‘Sterling Silver’ Tequila Extra Añejo, Jalisco, Mexico

This luxe bottling from Dos Armadillos is a twice-distilled tequila aged for over eight years. The ornate clay decanter is decorated with sterling silver.

  • Average price: $10,000
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Fruit jam, vanilla, oak

6. Patrón Limited Edition En Lalique Serie 3 Tequila Extra Añejo, Jalisco, Mexico

Patrón’s third series of its En Lalique lineup released in 2022 and is an extra añejo housed in crystal decanters.

  • Average price: $10,947
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Honey, dried fruit, oak

5. Clase Azul Master Artisans Canela Limited Edition Tequila, Jalisco, Mexico

Clase Azul’s Canela from the Master Artisans series is an extra añejo finished in ex-American whiskey, ex-amontillado sherry, and ex-Madeira casks.

  • Average price: $15,001
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Cooked agave, dark chocolate, caramel

4. Clase Azul ‘Jalisco 200’ Limited Edition Tequila Extra Añejo, Jalisco, Mexico

Clase Azul crafted the aptly named Jalisco 200 to commemorate the bicentennial of Jalisco as a Mexican state.

  • Average price: $12,651
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Molasses, honey, roasted agave

3. Clase Azul Master Artisans Guirnalda Limited Edition Tequila, Jalisco, Mexico

Guirnalda from Clase Azul’s Master Artisans lineup was aged for over eight years, moving from American whiskey casks to sherry barrels to finishing in Madeira casks.

  • Average price: $13,200
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Fig, almond, oak

2. Clase Azul Master Artisans Cobalto Limited Edition Tequila, Jalisco, Mexico

Another expression from Clase Azul’s Master Artisans collection, the Cobalto was created in collaboration with master artisan Jesús Guerrero Santos.

  • Average price: $15,001
  • ABV: 40%

content:
Unlike the approachably sweet vanilla and caramel flavors of corn-based bourbon, rye whiskey’s unique base delivers a distinct spice note that might turn off some first-timers. But once immersed in the category, rye’s savory qualities make it an essential tool in an at-home bartending arsenal, ideal for adding an extra kick to any whiskey cocktail.

Though bourbon may be the go-to gateway whiskey, bartenders celebrate — and sometimes prefer — rye for its more robust, complex taste. Those behind the stick are most attuned to the variety of rye whiskeys available and know the specific bottles that are most welcoming to newcomers’ palates. That’s why we asked 11 bartenders to name the rye whiskey they think is the best bet for a newbie. From well-known brands to small-batch distilleries, here’s what they had to say.

The best rye for beginners, according to bartenders:

  • Michter’s US*1 Rye
  • Elijah Craig Rye
  • Rittenhouse Rye Bottled-in-Bond
  • Bulleit Rye
  • Knob Creek 7 Year Old Rye
  • Fort Hamilton Single Barrel Rye Whiskey
  • Woodford Reserve Rye
  • Sazerac Rye

“My recommendation for a beginner rye whiskey would be Michter’s US*1 Rye. Many people approach rye expecting an intensely spicy or pepper-forward whiskey, but Michter’s offers a much softer introduction to the category. It delivers classic rye character while maintaining a rounded profile of caramel, vanilla, orange peel, baking spice, and light oak. What makes it particularly approachable is its balance: It has enough rye spice to demonstrate what sets the category apart from bourbon, but not so much that it becomes polarizing for newer whiskey drinkers. Whether enjoyed neat, on a large cube, or in a Manhattan or Old Fashioned, it provides an excellent foundation for understanding rye whiskey.” —Zack Flack, head bartender, The National, Autograph Collection, Oklahoma City

“Elijah Craig Rye is a fantastic place to start for beginners entering the rye world. To me, rye whiskey is like the cooler cousin to bourbon: It’s more sophisticated, nuanced, and flavorful compared to most entry-level bourbons. Elijah Craig Rye is not only marked at an affordable price, making it easy for your wallet, but also at a higher-than-average proof, which shines in cocktails or just over some ice.” —Zachariah Brown, head bartender, Point Seven, New York City

“I believe Rittenhouse Rye is the perfect starter rye. I naturally reach for higher-proof spirits when building cocktails, and at 100 proof, this one always fits the bill without getting lost. Its affordability and accessibility make it an easy choice, while the notes of dried fruit and lingering warm spice hit every fall craving. Sitting at exactly 51 percent rye, it’s the perfect ‘bridge’ whiskey for future enthusiasts.” —Stephanie Cohen, head bartender, The Port of Call, Mystic, Conn.

“Bulleit Rye is my choice for introducing beginners to rye whiskey, as its versatility works beautifully across applications. The flavor profile is compelling and accessible, presenting a clear range of flavors that are easy to understand while reflecting the classic characteristics found in traditional rye whiskey. At Millie Leigh’s, we’re aging Bulleit Rye in four-gallon casks for a few months to provide something different to our guests with the possibility of enjoying this rye in our version of an Old Fashioned made with vanilla syrup.” —Hugo Duffaut, beverage manager, Millie Leigh’s, Midland, Texas

“If I’m reaching for what I’d consider a beginner friendly rye, I’m assuming it’s for a bourbon drinker who’s ready to make the jump. Knob Creek 7 Year Old Rye ticks all the boxes for me. It has a high-corn mash bill which helps temper some of that rye spice and makes for an easier transition for most bourbon drinkers. It’s bottled at 100 proof with a seven year age statement, so there’s no shortage of complexity, texture, or weight on the palate without being too hot. And as far as value, Knob Creek has been punching above its weight in terms of quality versus price. Start with Knob Creek, and if you like what you see and are ready to graduate, cross the river to Indiana and check out some of the MGP bottlings next.” —Beck Hargrave, bartender, Oiji Mi, NYC

“Bulleit Rye is the best rye whiskey for beginners because of its approachable yet classic flavor profile. Known for its high-rye content — 95 percent rye and 5 percent malted barley — it offers a crisp, spicy character that defines the category. Despite the spice, it remains incredibly smooth, featuring gentle notes of vanilla, honey, and oak. This balance makes it smooth enough to sip neat, yet robust enough to stand out in classic cocktails like a Manhattan or an Old Fashioned. Affordable and widely available, it is the perfect introduction to rye!” —Valentin Bouteiller, bartender, Local 101 Beaurepaire, Paris

“Fort Hamilton Single Barrel Rye is a perfect choice for the beginner rye drinker. Distilled in Brooklyn, N.Y., from a mash bill of 90 percent rye and 10 percent malted barley and aged for minimum of five years, this 45 percent ABV rye is very approachable — it’s spicy but balanced with enough alcohol to show ‘character’ but without cask-strength intensity. You can detect caramel, cinnamon, mint, white pepper, oak, and lemon. It’s exceptionally rich with lots of texture and perfect for cocktails or to sip neat.” —Amir Babayoff, beverage director, Ophelia Lounge, NYC

“I would tell folks to start with the brand of bourbon they like and see if the same distillery also produces rye. I really enjoy Knob Creek Rye as an intro — it’s sweet but runs a tad hot with complexity emerging as you drink. Other ones would be Woodford Reserve Rye and Sazerac Rye. A good price range to stick to is $35 to $75 a bottle. Some may say it’s pedestrian, but I say drink what you like.” —Danielle Goldtooth, founder, Dii IINÀ, Phoenix

“Rittenhouse is great for beginners because it mixes so well. It’s a little higher proof, but that just means more rye flavor comes through. Cut it with a bit of cognac in a Sazerac, and you won’t be disappointed.” —Ian Alexander, beverage director, Limo Bar, NYC

“For beginners, I think Michter’s Rye is a great place to start. The mash bill is relatively low in rye, so while you still get that characteristic spice that you expect, it still feels a little more approachable for people who might be more accustomed to drinking bourbon. It holds up in classic rye-based cocktails but can also be enjoyed on its own without being overwhelming.” —Kat Foster, beverage director, Marlow East, NYC

“Rittenhouse Rye Bottled-in-Bond is a great starter rye because it’s approachable, affordable, and still gives you that classic spicy rye character. At 100 proof, it has enough backbone to stand up to vermouth, bitters, citrus, and other bold cocktail ingredients without getting lost, making it an absolute workhorse behind the bar.” —Libby Lingua, owner and bartender, Highball, Phoenix

content:
A problem — the problem? — for first-generation craft breweries is as follows.

1. Everybody knows your iconic beer.
2. Everybody loves your iconic beer.
3. Nobody buys your iconic beer.

We have contemplated this paradox many times here at Hop Take over the years. Recall the disastrous redesign Sapporo USA Sapporo Stone Brewing Sapporo USA put poor Anchor Brewing Company through at the beginning of this decade. Lament the ignominious demise of the original source of Leinenkugel’s beloved shandy. Bear witness to the regrettable unraveling of Rogue Ales & Spirits. And so on and so forth.

Complicating matters, pioneering breweries face a double-bind as they try to breathe new life into old brands. I framed up the problem in January 2023 about New Belgium Brewery’s then-new facelift for Fat Tire:

If Fat Tire were an actual bicycle, most people would put it on Craigslist and call it a day. But New Belgium can’t toss its former glory on the junk heap just yet. Even as younger drinkers gravitate toward the Voodoo Ranger clan’s bolder flavors and packaging, there are plenty of Gen Xers and Millennials with plenty of money for whom Fat Tire represents the golden era of early 21st-century American craft brewing. People still drink it! And despite its diminished stature, Fat Tire is still a top-20 craft brand overall. So New Belgium went for an overhaul instead, reformulating a “crisper, brighter” liquid and giving it a slick new package that calls attention to its eco-friendly credentials and omits its middling 5 percent ABV and outmoded style. “There’s a challenge to recharge heritage brands,” New Belgium vice president of marketing Kyle Bradshaw told Brewbound earlier this month, adding that the move “feels like a big risk” given Fat Tire’s outsized legacy.

That’s the rub. The American drinking public likes the idea of these classic craft beers much more than it actually likes buying them. To tinker with them too much is to invite much nostalgic gnashing of teeth; to leave them entirely untinkered with, to embrace decline.

Next year, Sierra Nevada Brewing Company — purveyor of the eponymous, irreproachable Pale Ale since 1980 — will take its biggest steps yet down the middle path. It’s been a long time coming.

“Five or six years ago when I started with Sierra, you know, one of the things that we were having to overcome was this perception of being ‘grocery store craft,’” says Kyle Ingram, Sierra Nevada’s senior director of innovation, in a phone interview with Hop Take. “Which is not quite an endearing term, not one that we were super proud of.”

The California outfit, which just last year edged out fellow first-waver Boston Beer Company in Brewers Association-defined craft beer barrelage, worked the problem from multiple angles. It recently unveiled its plans to refresh the packaging on a slate of core portfolio brands, including — gasp — Pale Ale itself in fall 2027. “Our portfolio had developed over such a long period of time that it didn’t look coherent on display, and I think some of it had aged and we needed to shake the dust off,” Sierra Nevada chief executive Pryce Greenow explained to Brewbound at a wholesaler conference at its North Carolina plant last month.

It bears mentioning that the company is actually embarking on that tightrope walk from a position of relative strength. According to multi-outlet grocery, mass retail, and convenience stores tracked by the market-research firm Circana, Sierra Nevada’s portfolio grew 1.9 percent in dollars and 0.2 percent in case volume year-to-date through September 6, outpacing the declining category and the even-more-rapidly declining craft segment within it.

Perhaps emboldened by that trend-bucking performance, the invigoration effort won’t stop with refreshes, though. “When you have a healthy core, it allows you to innovate in a way where we’re not dependent on that [new] thing being big and successful right out of the gate,” says Ingram.

To that end, Sierra Nevada has cued up two of its boldest portfolio expansions in recent memory. Crafted By Sierra Nevada, a line featuring “spiked agave seltzer” (read: hard seltzer) Agua Azul and “beer soda” (read: radler) Shred, marks the firm’s first major foray into the “beyond beer” space since it spun up and wound down also-ran entrants Tea West and Strainge Beast earlier this decade. The new fermentables are already on (or soon to hit) shelves in test markets bearing subordinated branding from the mothership.

“The question has always been can we win in those spaces without leveraging the awareness and the credibility of the Sierra Nevada brand, but also to do so without disparaging or diluting the equity of the Sierra Nevada brand for a loyal beer drinker?” says Ingram, to whom fell the unenviable responsibility of pitching founder Ken Grossman on a beer soda called Shred. “I remember thinking distinctly, this might be my last pitch,” he tells Hop Take, laughing.

Whether Craft By Sierra Nevada’s offerings can thrive — or even survive — in a lucrative-but-tricky flavored malt beverage pseudosegment dominated by scaled flavor-chasers like Mark Anthony Group, Anheuser-Busch InBev, and BBC remains to be seen. But to your humble Hop Take columnist’s eye, the thesis on those products is sound.

This brings us to the Hidden Scroll series. Unlike Crafted By, this new “brand family” is composed of honest-to-goodness beers, but it is tasked with a more ambitious goal. Namely: to score big, consistent Sierra Nevada some of the lucre and latter-day cachet of small, dynamic “hype breweries.”

“That guy who is paying 25 bucks for a four-pack, he’s looking for some of the more local, the more ‘hype’ kind of breweries in that space,” says Ingram. “We’re certainly capable and credible from a brewing standpoint, but maybe that’s not the area of the shelf or the cooler where people are looking for Sierra Nevada.” Building on the promise of West Ghost India Pale Ale — a semi-branded offering that made the transition from taproom-only bestseller to national packaged distribution in early 2026 — the company has formalized its higher-pricepoint ambitions under Hidden Scroll, so named because beers under this aegis will not feature the venerable gold sheafing that adorns labels in the core portfolio.

“That’s the first thing we want people to see, it’s the thing that brings that credibility, but we weren’t sure that it was working to our advantage in this space,” says Ingram of the scroll design. Instead: “Let’s grab shoppers’ attention with really cool modern artwork, because that’s a lot of how these guys shop.” He should know — by his own admission, he’s one of them.

For 2027, Sierra Nevada has retooled West Ghost’s packaging, and is deliberating over which of the other Hidden Scrolls beers it’s been testing in its taprooms it will put into 4-packs and push into distribution. Potential options include Boat Plane, a West Coast Pilsner, and Lava Lamp, a double IPA. The cans feature art-forward designs printed on the white matte labeling that’s become a visual lingua franca among more specialty craft offerings. There’s very little obvious connection to the brewery from whence they came but for a “Sierra Nevada Brewing Co., Chico, CA & Mills River, NC” demarcation along the bottom in small letters, and a faint scroll that’s been blended — hidden — into the illustration.

“People aren’t grabbing it because it’s from Sierra Nevada, they’re finding out that it’s from Sierra Nevada after they’ve already thrown a couple back,” says Ingram. “It’s been wildly successful for us, relative to the size of the category. We had a hard time keeping up with the volume in the first few months.”

Here, another rub. A core appeal of “hype” beers — to the extent that such appeal still exists at scale as we enter the back half of the ‘20s — is their scarcity, esotericism, and rapid-fire release cadence. Would, say, Other Half Brewing Company’s offerings have captivated finance bros late last decade if they were available in a dozen states, rather than only via a hole-in-the-wall across the street from a McDonald’s in central Brooklyn? Or, asked another way, is that sort of “hype” compatible with a Sierra Nevada sort of craft brewery?

I ask Ingram to square this circle.

For all Sierra Nevada’s logistical and technical advantages, “we have some disadvantages too. We’re not built to do small things really, really fast,” he concedes. “We’re not really designed to. That’s not the game that we’re playing, but we still feel like we can have a meaningful place in this category.”

Can Hidden Scroll find a place among the hype beer pantheon? Can Crafted By Sierra Nevada succeed where previous beyond-beer bids have failed? Can this four-decade firm bust the double-bind that has hemmed in so many craft beer brands of a certain age? Sierra Nevada has put together a compelling case. But only John Q. Guzzler can make the call.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

It’s no secret that Boston Beer Company has struggled mightily marketing-wise over the past few years. So the fact that it has a new chief marketing officer lined up isn’t surprising. But Allison Stransky, who starts October 12, has a resume that ought to raise some eyebrows: she’s taking this job after serving as the marketing lead for Samsung Electronics America. Can you pitch Samuel Adams the same way you pitch smartphones? Trade wisdom holds that you cannot. But we’ll see!

📈 Ups…

BBC taproom workers in Boston voted “overwhelmingly” to join the Teamsters… The THC drinks industry scored a brief stay of execution earlier this month when President Trump signed a bill kicking the can(nabis) to mid-December… New Belgium Brewery announced plans to open a “Liquid Center” (i.e., taproom) at Voodoo Ranger’s plant in Virginia…

📉 …and downs

Farewell to Mary Guiver, the longtime beer lead at Whole Foods Market, who’s moving to another role within the Amazon-owned grocer… Tilray Brands partnered with Spirit Halloween for a Shock Top promotion nobody asked for… More tough news from the Twin Cities, where top-50 firm Summit Brewing faces foreclosure… Rest in peace to Triple Rock, the country’s longest continuously operating brewpub, which is slated to shut its doors in Berkeley…

title: A Restaurant’s Off-Menu Wine List Should Feel Special, Not Exclusive
summary:
When I travel, I tend to go a bit extreme in my research of where I should eat and drink. Years ago, before taking a trip to Amsterdam, it was no different. During my weeks of research, I stumbled upon a new spot whose Instagram feed was chock full of wine nerd clickbait, but one post in particular caught my eye: “These Gems are Hiding in Our Wine Room: Kenjiro Kagami’s Domaine des Miroirs.” Naturally, I wanted to raid that wine room.

The article A Restaurant’s Off-Menu Wine List Should Feel Special, Not Exclusive appeared first on VinePair.
content:
When I travel, I tend to go a bit extreme in my research of where I should eat and drink. Years ago, before taking a trip to Amsterdam, it was no different. During my weeks of research, I stumbled upon a new spot whose Instagram feed was chock full of wine nerd clickbait, but one post in particular caught my eye: “These Gems are Hiding in Our Wine Room: Kenjiro Kagami’s Domaine des Miroirs.” Naturally, I wanted to raid that wine room.

We arrived at the restaurant and cafe, and I dug through the list only to find it was not there. I assumed someone had the same idea I had, came in, and bought it. I could find another wine, but I had to ask. What followed was my first true experience with the “off list” wine. It was an interrogation, albeit a very kind and hospitable one.

“How do you know this wine?”

“What do you know about this wine and its winemaker?”

“Have you ever had this wine before?”

“Are there other producers from this region that you really love?”

“What other wines are you really into right now?”

“Are there other wines that you see on the list that interest you?”

Some of these questions were things a somm may ask a guest when trying to figure out what wines to suggest, but this was different. It was a test, a very polite test, but a test all the same. Ultimately, I passed, after which it was explained, apologetically, that the restaurant only received a few bottles a year and they wanted to make sure each went to someone who would appreciate it.

The wine was great, the meal was great, and the service was solid. Overall, it was a great meal, though, to be honest, it did strike me as a bit odd and a little off-putting in the beginning. While this wine was definitely culty and nerdy at that time, it had yet to reach the unicorn status it has now. They did post the wine publicly, and that alone would attract people who appreciate it. It was most likely meant to bring in wine lovers like myself to the space, so why gatekeep it?

I’d mostly forgotten about this experience until a friend told me about something similar that had recently happened to him in Manhattan.

He went to a well known restaurant, and one of the servers recognized him immediately as a wine professional and let him know they had some amazing “off list” wines. He ordered one of the wines and loved it. He went back a few weeks later and inquired about the wine, but this time he had a different server.

“That wine isn’t on the list. Where did you have it?”

“Here.”

“Who served it to you?”

“Another server, I don’t remember his name.”

“Here?”

“Yes, here.”

After a pause, there was a, “Yeah, we have it.”

Mind you, this was not a unicorn $500 bottle with only two cases imported to the United States. It was a sub $100 wine from an unsung appellation. Needless to say, it left a bit of a bad taste in my friend’s mouth.

I was amazed by the absurdity and frustration of it, but the story brought me back to Amsterdam. What would my experience have been if I hadn’t answered the questions correctly? Would they have denied me? How would I have felt? Would I have been embarrassed? One thing is certain: I would not have felt better about myself or my experience at the restaurant, and I’m guessing others would not feel great about it either.

I want to lay this out from a hospitality perspective. I’m of the school that everyone should get a wonderful and equitable experience at a restaurant or bar, and that everyone should feel like they are getting something special. Having a separate list just for regulars and wine nerds goes against that.

Daniel Eddy of Brooklyn’s celebrated Winner and Runner Up has long talked about having a separate list, though he doesn’t view the potential list as a secret. He looks at it in a similar way to a rewards program punch card. If a guest dines with them five or 10 times, they would “unlock” a special list with rare, allocated bottles at a fair, nongouged price. He sees the possibility as more of a known reward for consistent patronage.

His reasoning is that he has a pretty deep list of special, hard to get wines at below market prices. Some are his personal consignments. When he first opened, there were several guests who would come in, cherry pick all the special wines, and never come back again. “I’d rather reward those who become regulars than let the cherry-pickers clean out the list and never return,” he says. As of today, he has not implemented this strategy but hopes to someday soon.

I get it. Wine directors don’t get many bottles of certain wines, and they want them to go to people who will both enjoy and appreciate them. You also want your regulars to feel special, but I don’t love the practice. How do you handle the guest who asks for the “secret list,” but isn’t a regular or someone you know? They clearly know about the list. They’re asking. How can you be hospitable in that situation?

I know of a restaurant where somms are instructed to tell guests a listed bottle is 86’d if the wine director doesn’t know the guest or thinks they don’t “deserve” the wine. It’s crazy to me that this happens, but sadly it does, and this type of gatekeeping is exactly why wine is struggling these days.

If you list a wine, everyone should be able to buy it, regardless of their knowledge of wine. Most guests who come in aren’t going to know as much as the somm, and yes, the somm can and should try to steer people toward wines they think the guest will love and away from wines they may not enjoy as much. But if the guest sees something on the list and wants to pay for it, it should not be withheld. It’s bad business among other things.

None of this is without caveats. I would be lying if I said I never sold off-list wines. I have. At my restaurant LaLou, we had plenty of wines that were not listed for a variety of reasons.

Some wines needed time and were purposely held in the cellar until we thought they were ready to go. Occasionally, someone would come in and want that particular style of wine. We might sell them a bottle with the understanding that “it might be a bit tight” or “it’s a bit young, but let’s see where it’s at.”

Some wine lists only have a limited amount of space, and some places will keep wines off because they simply don’t have room and are waiting for another wine to run out before they can print it. I would 100 percent sell that wine off-list to a guest who was looking for something similar. Sometimes I would sell wines that had just arrived and we had not had time to list them, but I would sell the wine based on the guest’s preferences, not on who the guest was or what they did or didn’t know about the wine.

It’s important to note that these wines were not on a separate “cool kids,” industry or regulars list. They were offered to any guests who were not finding what they wanted on our list, and we were attempting to give them a special experience. It wasn’t a strategic “special list” for certain guests. It was happenstance that allowed us to do this, and I think that is the main point.

Here, it’s the intent that counts. Hospitality is giving people something they didn’t know they wanted. A special list for the worthy or those in the know is antithetical to that. It doesn’t create new regulars, it rewards the current ones while running the risk of alienating potential ones.

At a moment when we are barraged with stories that hospitality is at a breaking point and wine consumption is at a breaking point, that restaurants are going out of business, and grape growers are ripping out vines, we should be thinking of ways to get more people in the doors and drinking more wine, not excluding guests and potential wine drinkers.
